claim: Complex systems are challenging to understand, especially when they defy manipulative experiments for practical or ethical reasons.
source: Complex systems are challenging to understand, especially when they defy manipulative experiments for practical or ethical reasons.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenges of studying complex systems, drawing on established scientific knowledge about experimental limitations.

claim: Several fields have developed parallel approaches to infer causal relations from observational time series.
source: Several fields have developed parallel approaches to infer causal relations from observational time series.
evidence: This statement is supported by the existence of the methods discussed in the manuscript and references to multiple fields.

claim: Statistical causal discovery methods are easy to misunderstand and often controversial.
source: Yet, these methods are easy to misunderstand and often controversial.
evidence: The manuscript later provides citations to controversial exchanges in the literature.

claim: Ecological communities perform important activities, from facilitating digestion in the human gut to driving biogeochemical cycles.
source: Ecological communities perform important activities, from facilitating digestion in the human gut to driving biogeochemical cycles.
evidence: This draws on established scientific knowledge about the roles of ecological communities.

claim: Communities are often highly complex, with many species engaging in diverse interactions.
source: Communities are often highly complex, with many species engaging in diverse interactions.
evidence: This is based on established ecological knowledge.

claim: To control communities, it helps to know causal relationships between variables.
source: To control communities, it helps to know causal relationships between variables (e.g. whether perturbing the abundance of one species might alter the abundance of another species).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the utility of causal knowledge for control.

claim: Causal relationships can be expressed explicitly by proposing causal networks.
source: We can express these relationships either explicitly by proposing causal networks (Spirtes and Zhang, 2016; Chattopadhyay et al., 2019; Glymour et al., 2019; Runge et al., 2019b; Runge et al., 2019a; Sanchez-Romero et al., 2019; Leng et al., 2020), or implicitly by simply predicting the effects of new perturbations (Daniels and Nemenman, 2015; Mangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on causal networks.

claim: Causal relationships can be expressed implicitly by predicting the effects of new perturbations.
source: We can express these relationships either explicitly by proposing causal networks (Spirtes and Zhang, 2016; Chattopadhyay et al., 2019; Glymour et al., 2019; Runge et al., 2019b; Runge et al., 2019a; Sanchez-Romero et al., 2019; Leng et al., 2020), or implicitly by simply predicting the effects of new perturbations (Daniels and Nemenman, 2015; Mangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on prediction-based approaches.

claim: Manipulative experiments can be infeasible or inappropriate for natural ecosystems.
source: However, manipulative experiments can be infeasible or inappropriate: Natural ecosystems may not offer enough replicates for comprehensive manipulative experiments, and perturbations can be impractical at large scales and may have unanticipated negative consequences.
evidence: This is based on practical knowledge about ecological research constraints.

claim: There exists an ever-growing abundance of observational time series.
source: On the other hand, there exists an ever-growing abundance of observational time series (i.e. without intentional perturbations).
evidence: This is an observation about trends in data availability in science.

claim: The Lotka-Volterra model assumes that species interact in a pairwise fashion.
source: For example, the Lotka-Volterra model popular in mathematical ecology assumes that species interact in a pairwise fashion, that the fitness effects from different interactions are additive, and that all pairwise interactions can be represented by a single equation form where parameters can vary to reflect signs and strengths of fitness effects.
evidence: This describes a well-known property of the Lotka-Volterra model.

claim: The Lotka-Volterra model assumes that fitness effects from different interactions are additive.
source: For example, the Lotka-Volterra model popular in mathematical ecology assumes that species interact in a pairwise fashion, that the fitness effects from different interactions are additive, and that all pairwise interactions can be represented by a single equation form where parameters can vary to reflect signs and strengths of fitness effects.
evidence: This describes a well-known property of the Lotka-Volterra model.

claim: Fitting the Lotka-Volterra model to time series can predict which species interact or how a community might respond to perturbations.
source: By fitting such a model to time series of species abundances and environmental factors, one can predict, for instance, which species interact or how a community might respond to certain perturbations (Stein et al., 2013; Fisher and Mehta, 2014; Bucci et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works that have applied this approach.

claim: The Lotka-Volterra equations often fail to describe complex ecosystems and chemically mediated interactions.
source: However, the Lotka-Volterra equations often fail to describe complex ecosystems and chemically mediated interactions (Levine, 1976; Wootton, 2002; Momeni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works documenting these failures.

claim: Model-free methods typically rely on statistical models.
source: Such methods are sometimes called 'model-free' (Coenen et al., 2020), although they typically rely on statistical models.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of so-called model-free methods, with a citation.

claim: Some causal discovery methods examine 'information flow' between time series without using equation-based descriptions.
source: Some of these methods avoid any equation-based description of the dynamics and instead examine some notion of 'information flow' between time series (Granger, 1980; Sugihara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works using information flow concepts.

claim: Some causal discovery methods deploy highly flexible equations that are not necessarily mechanistic.
source: Others deploy highly flexible equations that are not necessarily mechanistic (Granger, 1969; Barnett and Seth, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works using flexible equation-based approaches.

claim: Modern causal discovery approaches have intellectual roots in several communities including philosophy, statistics, econometrics, and chaos theory.
source: First, modern causal discovery approaches have intellectual roots in several communities including philosophy, statistics, econometrics, and chaos theory, which sometimes use different words for the same idea, and the same word for different ideas.
evidence: This is a historical observation about the development of causal discovery methods.

claim: Different communities sometimes use different words for the same idea in causal discovery.
source: First, modern causal discovery approaches have intellectual roots in several communities including philosophy, statistics, econometrics, and chaos theory, which sometimes use different words for the same idea, and the same word for different ideas.
evidence: This is an observation about terminology differences across fields.

claim: Key assumptions in methodological articles are sometimes hidden in algorithmic details or not mentioned.
source: A second challenge is that in methodological articles, key assumptions are sometimes hidden in algorithmic details, or simply not mentioned.
evidence: This is an observation about methodological literature practices.

claim: Some causal discovery methods deal with nuanced or advanced mathematical ideas that can be difficult even for those with quantitative training.
source: Finally, some methods deal with nuanced or advanced mathematical ideas that can be difficult even for those with quantitative training.
evidence: This is an observation about the complexity of certain methods.

claim: Efforts to infer causal relationships from observational time series have sometimes been highly controversial.
source: Given these challenges, it is no surprise that efforts to infer causal relationships from observational time series have sometimes been highly controversial, with an abundance of 'letters to the editor', sometimes followed by impassioned dialogue (Luo et al., 2015; Baskerville and Cobey, 2017; Tiokhin and Hruschka, 2017; Schaller et al., 2017; Barnett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to controversial exchanges in the literature.

claim: Whether a causer is direct or indirect can depend on the scope of included variables.
source: Whether a causer is direct or indirect can depend on the scope of included variables.
evidence: This is illustrated with an example about yeast, acetate, and bacteria.

claim: The term 'correlation' is often used to describe some statistic that quantifies the similarity between two observed time series.
source: When applied to ecological time series, the term 'correlation' is often used to describe some statistic that quantifies the similarity between two observed time series (Weiss et al., 2016; Coenen and Weitz, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works using correlation in this way.

claim: Statistical dependence is a hypothesis about the probability distributions that produced time series and has close connections to causality.
source: In contrast, statistical dependence is a hypothesis about the probability distributions that produced those time series, and has close connections to causality.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction made by the authors.

claim: The Common Cause Principle states that if two variables are dependent, then they are causally related.
source: Dependence is connected to causation by the widely accepted 'Common Cause Principle': if two variables are dependent, then they are causally related (i.e. one causes the other, or both share a common cause; Peters et al., 2017; Runge et al., 2019a; Hitchcock, 2020b; Hitchcock and Rédei, 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on causal principles.

claim: If one mistakenly introduces selection bias, then two independent variables can appear to be dependent.
source: Note however that if one mistakenly introduces selection bias, then two independent variables can appear to be dependent (Appendix 2—figure 3).
evidence: This is illustrated in Appendix 2—figure 3.

claim: When conditional dependence and conditional independence relationships are known, it is sometimes possible to infer most or all of the direct causal relationships at play.
source: In fact, when conditional dependence (and conditional independence) relationships are known, it is sometimes possible to infer most or all of the direct causal relationships at play, even without manipulative experiments or temporal information.
evidence: This is a statement about the power of conditional dependence analysis.

claim: Many algorithms for inferring causal structure rely on the causal Markov condition and the causal faithfulness condition.
source: Many of the algorithms that accomplish this rely on two technical but often reasonable assumptions: the 'causal Markov condition', which allows one to infer causal information from conditional dependence, and the 'causal faithfulness condition', which allows one to infer causal information from conditional independence (Appendix 2; Peters et al., 2017; Glymour et al., 2019; Hitchcock, 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on causal discovery algorithms.

claim: Time series are often autocorrelated, so that a single pair of time series contains information from only a single trial.
source: This is because time series are often autocorrelated (e.g. what occurs today influences what occurs tomorrow), so that a single pair of time series contains information from only a single trial.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical properties of time series.

claim: Parametric tests using the Pearson correlation coefficient that account for autocorrelation rely on estimates of the autocorrelation at each lag for both time series, which can be highly uncertain.
source: However, the calculation of this variance relies on estimates of the autocorrelation at each lag for both time series, which can be highly uncertain (Pyper and Peterman, 1998; Ebisuzaki, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on autocorrelation estimation.

claim: If two time series are independent, surrogate data testing should register a p-value of 0.05 or less in only 5% of cases.
source: Ideally, if two time series are independent, then we should register a a p-value of 0.05 (or less) in only 5% of cases.
evidence: This is a statement about the expected behavior of a valid statistical test.

claim: Permutation assumes that all possible orderings of the time points in a series are equally likely.
source: This procedure, often called permutation, assumes that all possible orderings of the time points in the series are equally likely.
evidence: This describes the assumption underlying permutation testing.

claim: The permutation assumption is commonly violated in time series due to autocorrelation, and thus the test is often invalid.
source: This assumption is commonly violated in time series due to autocorrelation, and thus the test is often invalid.
evidence: This is an inference about the validity of permutation testing for autocorrelated data.

claim: Permutation testing has appeared in many applied works, perhaps because it has been the default option in some popular software packages.
source: Nevertheless, permutation testing has appeared in many applied works, perhaps because it has been the default option in some popular software packages.
evidence: This is speculation about why permutation testing is commonly used despite its problems.

claim: Phase randomization uses the Fourier transform to represent a time series as a sum of sine waves, then randomly shifts each component sine wave in time.
source: It first uses the Fourier transform to represent a time series as a sum of sine waves, then randomly shifts each of the component sine waves in time, and finally sums the phase-shifted components (Ebisuzaki, 1997; Schreiber and Schmitz, 2000; Andrzejak et al., 2003; Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This describes the phase randomization procedure with citations.

claim: Phase randomization is considered appropriate when the original time series is obtained from a linear, Gaussian, and stationary process.
source: This procedure is considered appropriate when the original time series is obtained from a linear, Gaussian, and stationary process (Andrzejak et al., 2003; Lancaster et al., 2018), where 'linear' means that future values depend linearly on past values, 'Gaussian' means that any subsequence follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution, and 'stationary' means that this distribution does not change over time.
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on phase randomization.

claim: Phase randomization performed well (with a false positive rate of 4%) when time series satisfied its assumptions.
source: Indeed, this test performed well (with a false positive rate of 4%) when time series satisfied its assumptions (Figure 2C), and poorly when the stationarity assumption was violated (with a false positive rate of 21%; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is data from simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Phase randomization performed poorly when the stationarity assumption was violated (with a false positive rate of 21%).
source: Indeed, this test performed well (with a false positive rate of 4%) when time series satisfied its assumptions (Figure 2C), and poorly when the stationarity assumption was violated (with a false positive rate of 21%; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is data from simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some surrogate data tests have been shown to perform reasonably well even when the exact theoretical requirements are unmet or unknown.
source: Some surrogate data tests have been shown to perform reasonably well even when the exact theoretical requirements are unmet or unknown (Thiel et al., 2006; Papana et al., 2017), but a more comprehensive benchmarking effort is needed to map out each method's valid domain in practice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on surrogate data testing.

claim: A more comprehensive benchmarking effort is needed to map out each surrogate data method's valid domain in practice.
source: Some surrogate data tests have been shown to perform reasonably well even when the exact theoretical requirements are unmet or unknown (Thiel et al., 2006; Papana et al., 2017), but a more comprehensive benchmarking effort is needed to map out each method's valid domain in practice.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: Granger causality excludes indirect causes.
source: An important consequence of this definition is that Granger causality excludes indirect causes, as illustrated in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Whether a causal relationship is direct or indirect depends on which variables are observed.
source: In practice, whether a causal relationship is direct or indirect depends on which variables are observed.
evidence: This is a conceptual point about the relativity of direct causation.

claim: If a system has deterministic dynamics, then Granger causality may fail to detect causal relations.
source: First, if a system has deterministic dynamics (see Appendix 3), then Granger causality may fail to detect causal relations (Figure 3Bi).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 3Bi.

claim: Granger causality may erroneously assign a direct causal relation between a pair of variables that have an unobserved common cause.
source: Second, Granger causality may erroneously assign a direct causal relation between a pair of variables that have an unobserved common cause (Figure 3Bii).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 3Bii.

claim: Recording data at a frequency below that of the original process can alter the inferred causal structure.
source: Third, recording data at a frequency below that of the original process by 'subsampling' (e.g. taking weekly measurements of a daily process) or by 'temporal aggregation' (e.g. taking weekly averages of a daily process) can alter the inferred causal structure (Figure 3Biii), although recent techniques can help with these issues (Gong et al., 2015; Hyttinen et al., 2016; Gong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 3Biii and supported by citations.

claim: When measurements are noisy, Granger causality can assign false interactions and also fail to detect true causality.
source: Lastly, when measurements are noisy (Figure 3Biv), Granger causality can assign false interactions and also fail to detect true causality (Newbold, 1978), although some progress has been made on this front (Nalatore et al., 2007).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 3Biv and supported by citations.

claim: Linear Granger causality has standard parametric tests available in multiple free and well-documented software packages.
source: Parametric tests are computationally inexpensive and available in multiple free and well-documented software packages (Seabold and Perktold, 2010; Barnett and Seth, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to software packages.

claim: Linear Granger causality tests assume that time series are covariance-stationary.
source: These tests assume that time series are 'covariance-stationary', which means that certain statistical properties of the series are time-independent (Barnett and Seth, 2014; see also Appendix 3), and can fail when this assumption is violated (Toda and Phillips, 1993; Ohanian, 1988; He and Maekawa, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on stationarity requirements.

claim: Linear Granger causality tests can fail when the covariance-stationarity assumption is violated.
source: These tests assume that time series are 'covariance-stationary', which means that certain statistical properties of the series are time-independent (Barnett and Seth, 2014; see also Appendix 3), and can fail when this assumption is violated (Toda and Phillips, 1993; Ohanian, 1988; He and Maekawa, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works documenting these failures.

claim: Applying linear Granger causality to nonlinear systems can lead to incorrect causal conclusions.
source: Additionally, applying linear Granger causality to nonlinear systems can lead to incorrect causal conclusions (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on this issue.

claim: Tests for general Granger causality often use a statistic known as transfer entropy.
source: Tests for general Granger causality often use a statistic known as transfer entropy (Papana et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on transfer entropy.

claim: A significant transfer entropy indicates the presence of general Granger causality.
source: A significant transfer entropy thus indicates the presence of general Granger causality.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of transfer entropy.

claim: Surrogate data are typically used to evaluate significance of transfer entropy.
source: Surrogate data are typically used to evaluate significance (Montalto et al., 2014; Papana et al., 2017; Shorten et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on transfer entropy testing.

claim: Previously discussed surrogate data procedures are designed to test the null hypothesis of independence, which is different from the null hypothesis of general Granger non-causality.
source: However, the previously discussed surrogate data procedures are designed to test the null hypothesis of independence, which is different from the null hypothesis of general Granger non-causality (i.e. Equation 2, but replace '≠' with '=').
evidence: This is an observation about the mismatch between null hypotheses.

claim: More recent surrogate procedures have been proposed to address the issue of testing for general Granger non-causality.
source: More recent surrogate procedures have been proposed to address this issue (Runge, 2018a; Shorten et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent methodological work.

claim: When datasets have a large number of variables, a regression procedure may fail to detect many true interactions.
source: Granger causality methods face challenges when datasets have a large number of variables (e.g. in microbial ecology). In this case, the summation in Equation 1 will contain a large number of terms, and so a regression procedure may fail to detect many true interactions (Runge et al., 2019a; Runge et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on high-dimensional causal discovery.

claim: To handle systems with many variables, one can impose the assumption that only a small number of causal links exist.
source: To handle systems with many variables, one can impose the assumption that only a small number of causal links exist (Gibbons et al., 2017; Mainali et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on sparse regression.

claim: Under certain technical assumptions, it is possible to use a series of logical rules to remove unnecessary terms in a purely data-driven way.
source: Additionally, under certain technical assumptions, it is possible to use a series of logical rules to remove unnecessary terms in a purely data-driven way (Runge et al., 2019b; Runge et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works on constraint-based causal discovery.

claim: SSR methods are intended to complement Granger causality by being explicitly designed for systems that are primarily deterministic.
source: SSR methods are intended to complement Granger causality: Whereas Granger causality has trouble with deterministic dynamics (Figure 3B), the SSR approach is explicitly designed for systems that are primarily deterministic (Sugihara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on SSR methods.

claim: Takens' theorem states that if a particle follows a deterministic trajectory which forms a surface, and if we take one-dimensional measurements of that particle's position over time, then we are almost guaranteed to find a continuous delay map from our measurements to the original surface, as long as we use enough delays.
source: A rough translation of Takens' theorem is the following: If a particle follows a deterministic trajectory which forms a surface (e.g. an ant crawling all over a doughnut), and if we take one-dimensional measurements of that particle's position over time (e.g. the distance from the ant's starting position), then we are almost guaranteed to find a continuous delay map from our measurements (of current distance) to the original surface (the donut), as long as we use enough delays.
evidence: This is a simplified explanation of Takens' theorem.

claim: We can typically expect to find continuous delay maps from dynamically driven variables to dynamically driving variables in a coupled deterministic dynamical system, as long as certain technical requirements are met.
source: A key result that follows from this theorem is that we can typically ('generically') expect to find continuous delay maps from 'dynamically driven' variables to 'dynamically driving' variables in a coupled deterministic dynamical system, as long as certain technical requirements are met (Cummins et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on SSR theory.

claim: In theory, Takens' theorem says that almost any choice of delay vector should work as long as it contains enough delays.
source: In theory, Takens' theorem says that almost any choice of delay vector should work as long as it contains enough delays.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical implications of Takens' theorem.

claim: In practice, with finite noisy data, the behavior of SSR methods can depend on the delay vector selection procedure.
source: However in practice, with finite noisy data, the behavior of SSR methods can depend on the delay vector selection procedure (Cobey and Baskerville, 2016; see also Appendix 4).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on SSR method sensitivity.

claim: While causation is one possible explanation for a continuous delay map, it is not the only possible explanation.
source: As a word of warning, while causation is one possible explanation for a continuous delay map, it is not the only possible explanation.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about interpreting continuous delay maps.

claim: The nonreverting continuous dynamics pathology may explain apparently causal results in some early works where SSR methods were applied to data with a clear temporal trend.
source: This pathology leads to false causal conclusions and may explain apparently causal results in some early works where SSR methods were applied to data with a clear temporal trend.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of false positives in early SSR applications.

claim: Clark et al., 2015 recommend shading points in the delay space with their corresponding time to visually check for a time trend.
source: We are not aware of statistical tests for this problem, but Clark et al., 2015 recommend shading points in the delay space with their corresponding time to visually check for a time trend.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recommendation in the literature.

claim: When one variable drives another variable in such a way that the dynamics of the two variables are synchronized, bidirectional causality is inferred even though the true causal relationship is unidirectional.
source: In the second failure mode (Figure 5, second row; see also Sugihara et al., 2012), one variable drives another variable in such a way that the dynamics of the two variables are synchronized. Consequently, although the true causal relationship is unidirectional, bidirectional causality is inferred.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 5 second row and supported by a citation.

claim: The prediction lag test can sometimes alleviate the synchrony problem, but it is not foolproof.
source: Although the 'prediction lag test' (Figure 6B right panel) can sometimes alleviate this problem (Ye et al., 2015; Cobey and Baskerville, 2016), it is not foolproof as we demonstrate in Appendix 4.
evidence: This is supported by citations and demonstrated in Appendix 4.

claim: SSR can give a false negative error due to pathological symmetry, although this may be rare in practice.
source: In the fourth failure mode (Figure 5, bottom row), SSR gives a false negative error due to 'pathological symmetry', although this may be rare in practice.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 5 bottom row.

claim: Convergent cross mapping (CCM) is the most popular SSR method for detecting causal signals.
source: Several methods have been used to detect SSR causal signals by detecting approximate continuity (Cummins et al., 2015) or related properties (Sugihara et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014; Harnack et al., 2017). The most popular is convergent cross mapping (CCM), which has been applied to nonlinear (Sugihara et al., 2012) or linear deterministic systems (Barraquand et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to works using CCM.

claim: CCM is based on a statistic called cross map skill that quantifies how well a causer can be predicted from delay vectors of its causee.
source: CCM is based on a statistic called 'cross map skill' that quantifies how well a causer can be predicted from delay vectors of its causee (Figure 6A), conceptually similar to checking for gradual transitions when shading the causee delay space by causer values (Figure 4).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: Four criteria have been proposed to infer causality from CCM: positive cross map skill, significant cross map skill, increasing cross map skill with more training data, and greater cross map skill when predicting past values than future values.
source: Four criteria have been proposed to infer causality (Sugihara et al., 2012; Ye et al., 2015; Cobey and Baskerville, 2016; Figure 6B): First, the cross map skill must be positive. Second, the cross map skill must be significant according to some surrogate data test. Third, the cross map skill must increase with an increasing amount of training data. Lastly, the cross map skill must be greater when predicting past values of the causer than when predicting future values of the causer (the prediction lag test [Ye et al., 2015; Cobey and Baskerville, 2016] in the right panel of Figure 6B, but see Appendix 4 for caveats of this test).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: Many CCM analyses use only a subset of the four criteria for inferring causality.
source: In practice, many if not most CCM analyses use only a subset of these four criteria (Sugihara et al., 2012; Brookshire and Weaver, 2015; Cramer et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to applied works.

claim: Other approaches to detect various aspects of continuous delay maps have been proposed.
source: Other approaches to detect various aspects of continuous delay maps have also been proposed (Ma et al., 2014; Cummins et al., 2015; Harnack et al., 2017; Leng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to alternative methods.

claim: There is no systematic comparison of alternative SSR methods for detecting continuous delay maps.
source: We do not know of a systematic comparison of these alternatives.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of comparative studies.

claim: Granger causality and CCM can perform well when their respective requirements are met.
source: Granger causality and CCM can perform well when their respective requirements are met, but both are fairly sensitive to the levels of process and measurement noise (Figure 7D and E, correct inferences colored as green in pie charts) and to details of the ecosystem (whether or not S2 has its own external driver; compare Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Both Granger causality and CCM are fairly sensitive to the levels of process and measurement noise.
source: Granger causality and CCM can perform well when their respective requirements are met, but both are fairly sensitive to the levels of process and measurement noise (Figure 7D and E, correct inferences colored as green in pie charts) and to details of the ecosystem (whether or not S2 has its own external driver; compare Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: In both Granger causality and CCM, detection of the true causal link is disrupted by either the strongest measurement noise or the strongest process noise used in the simulations.
source: In both methods, detection of the true causal link is disrupted by either the strongest measurement noise (standard deviation of 1) or the strongest process noise (standard deviation of 8) used here.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: For Granger causality, as measurement noise increases, process noise often needs to increase for Granger causality to perform well.
source: When process and/or measurement noise is present, their relative amount is important: As measurement noise increases (from bottom to top), process noise often needs to increase (from left to right) for Granger causality to perform well.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Measurement noise can induce false positives in Granger causality.
source: Indeed, prior analytical results (Newbold, 1978; Nalatore et al., 2007) show that measurement noise can induce false positives (e.g. red slices in row 2, column 2) and hide true positives (e.g. grey slices in row 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Measurement noise can hide true positives in Granger causality.
source: Indeed, prior analytical results (Newbold, 1978; Nalatore et al., 2007) show that measurement noise can induce false positives (e.g. red slices in row 2, column 2) and hide true positives (e.g. grey slices in row 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Increasing measurement noise can sometimes improve Granger causality performance.
source: Surprisingly, increasing measurement noise can sometimes improve performance (in column 3 of both panels, row two has a larger green slice than row 3).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: When S2 has its own external driver, there is no synchrony, and CCM performs admirably in the deterministic setting.
source: When S2 has its own external driver (Figure 7D), there is no synchrony, and CCM performs admirably in the deterministic setting (lower left corner).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7D.

claim: CCM performs less well when measurement or process noise is introduced.
source: CCM performs less well when measurement or process noise is introduced.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: When the external driver of S1 is removed, CCM performs poorly, likely because the two species are now synchronized in the absence of noise.
source: Strikingly, when we remove the external driver of S1 (Figure 7E), CCM performs poorly. This is likely because the two species are now synchronized in the absence of noise (violating the 'no synchrony' requirement of CCM).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7E and inference about the cause.

claim: Adding noise to a synchronized system removes the synchrony problem but violates the determinism requirement of CCM.
source: However, adding noise, which removes the synchrony problem, violates the determinism requirement. So CCM is frustrated either way.
evidence: This is an inference about the trade-off between CCM requirements.

claim: Unlike CCM, Granger causality is less sensitive to the presence of underlying synchrony as long as this synchrony is disrupted by process noise.
source: Note that unlike CCM, Granger causality is less sensitive to the presence of underlying synchrony as long as this synchrony is disrupted by process noise.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The performance of CCM is sensitive to the test procedure.
source: Additionally, the performance of CCM (Figure 7D and E, right panels) is sensitive to the test procedure (olive brackets).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Where a system lies in the spectrum of process versus measurement noise is often unknown.
source: In reality, where a system lies in the spectrum of process versus measurement noise is often unknown, and we are not aware of any method that reliably distinguishes between process noise and measurement noise without knowing the functional form of the system.
evidence: This is a statement about practical limitations in distinguishing noise types.

claim: There is no known method that reliably distinguishes between process noise and measurement noise without knowing the functional form of the system.
source: In reality, where a system lies in the spectrum of process versus measurement noise is often unknown, and we are not aware of any method that reliably distinguishes between process noise and measurement noise without knowing the functional form of the system.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of methods for noise type identification.

claim: Deterministic processes tend to be more predictable than stochastic processes, at least in the short term.
source: One idea is that deterministic processes tend to be more predictable than stochastic processes, at least in the short term (Hastings et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on predictability.
